evidence: Hor. C. 1.31.16: mē cichorēa levēsque malvae
terms.comment: Greek κιχώριον. Pliny says that cichorium is the Egyptian name of the wild intubus (NH 19.129; 20.73), and Morgan–Owens (after André and Jones) takes cichorium as chicory, Cichorium intybus, where intubus covered chicory and endive alike. Horace’s form is cichorēum.

terms.gloss: endive or chicory, the two not told apart
terms.comment: Lewis & Short heads it intibus, also intybus and intubus, masculine or feminine, and neuter intibum; we give the spelling of Pliny’s text. The wild plant, chicory, is intubum errāticum (NH 19.129) or intubus silvestris (Morgan–Owens, after Pliny NH 20.73).

phrases.latin: mē pāscunt olīvae, mē cichorēa levēsque malvae
phrases.english: my food is olives, chicory, and light mallows

phrases.latin: est et errāticum intubum, quod in Aegyptō cichorium vocant
phrases.english: there is also a wild endive, which in Egypt they call cichorium

sources: Lewis & Short: cichorium · Lewis & Short: intibus
